newsitem.title: UK: Surging world coffee prices hit consumers.
newsitem.headline: Surging world coffee prices hit consumers.

text.p: German roasters followed a lead given by the Dutch on Friday in deciding to raise retail coffee prices at the supermarket check-out in reaction to a sharp increase in the world price of coffee beans.

New York futures for Arabica beans rose to the highest in 17 months on Friday and London values for Robusta grades were trading close to $1,630 per tonne, up by almost one-third since the end of 1996, before end week profit-taking took the top off the market.
German roaster Kraft Jacobs Suchard (KJS) said it would raise the retail prices of its roasted coffee by two marks ($1.20) per kg effective March 10.
The world coffee market is up because stocks are low and Brazil's next crop may turn out lower than expected at around 20 million bags.
KJS is part of the Phillip Morris Co Inc. The German market leader cited higher raw material prices for the retail increase while rival German firms said they had similar plans.
A spokesman for premium roaster Alois Dallmayr Kaffee oHG in Munich said his firm had chosen a similar course of action.
"Coffee prices applying to our blends have nearly risen by 50 percent over the last two months and with the dollar higher as well it is inevitable for us to raise prices," he said.
The Dutch firm of Douwe Egberts raised prices on the shelf earlier this week and Japanese consumers may be next to pay more.

"Rising coffee bean prices and the weaker yen have sharply pushed up our costs and cut profit margins. The situation is getting tougher for us," said Akio Yamaoka, a spokesman for UCC Ueshima Coffee Co Ltd of Japan.
The supply worries were heightened by news of a debt repayment strike declared on Wednesday by Colombia's independent coffee growers.

Traders in London said that although this would not impact supplies in the short-term, there could be adverse implications if creditor banks foreclose on mortgages and seize control of about 50,000 plantations.
Elsewhere in world commodity markets gold extended its inexorable decline as investors continue to abandon it because of fears that central banks may sell more bullion from their reserves.
Gold slid below $340 an ounce in London, a decline of some $30 since the start of 1997.
Oil prices, after a long bull run, also seem to be easing. Light crude traded in New York slipped below $23 per barrel for the first time in five months.
Bellwether North Sea Brent crude futures traded in London were below $21.25 late in the British afternoon.
"You are seeing prices taking their cue from a declining heating oil market, which is in turn a function of weather being warmer than normal," says Mike Rothman, oil analyst with Merrill Lynch.
